summary: Describes the Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) version 1.0, a framework meant to let different electronic commerce systems interoperate. It aims to give consumers, merchants and payment providers a common way to run purchases online. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Shops and payment systems often speak different languages. This describes a common way for them to talk, so you can buy something online the same way no matter who is selling or handling the payment.

questions: what are the iotp trading exchanges
subtitle: An XML framework for online trades that stays the same whichever payment system, merchant or delivery service is involved.

tldr.problem: Online buying and selling involves several parties (shop, payment provider, delivery firm, support) and many incompatible payment systems, so software from different vendors could not trade with each other.
tldr.mechanism: IOTP defines XML messages built from Trading Blocks and Trading Components that carry an offer, a payment, a delivery or an authentication between named Trading Roles, and wraps the payment system's own messages without changing them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo describing Baseline IOTP version 1.0, a deliberately limited set of eight transaction types. It does not set an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2801 is an Informational memo, so it does not specify an Internet standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies Baseline IOTP version 1.0 and points to separate supplements for payment schemes and transports; signatures are covered in more detail by RFC 2802.

sections.title: Why IOTP Exists
sections.content:
The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) is described as an interoperable framework for Internet commerce. It is payment system independent and encapsulates payment systems such as SET, Mondex, CyberCash, DigiCash and GeldKarte. It can handle cases where the shopping site, the Payment Handler, the Delivery Handler and the customer support provider are one party or several different ones.

The RFC says the aim is to replicate in the virtual world the familiar steps of real trade: agreeing who is involved, presenting an offer, paying, getting a receipt and receiving the goods. It names three goals: familiar trading models, new trading models and global interoperability. It also lists how trade online differs from the physical world: the parties are rarely face to face, authentication is harder, very small payments become possible, and goods can be delivered electronically.

This document is Baseline IOTP. It covers the most common trades, such as purchases and refunds, and the authors expected no scope changes in the meantime, only corrections. The RFC states that it does not address legal or regulatory issues, and that it does not prescribe the software each participant must build.
sections.eli5: Shops, banks and delivery people all do different jobs and speak different languages. IOTP is a shared language so any shop and any bank can still finish a sale together.

sections.title: The Five Trading Roles
sections.content:
IOTP describes a trade in terms of Trading Roles, not companies. A single organisation can play one role or all of them, and a company can be a Merchant when selling and a Consumer when buying.

  • Consumer: receives and pays for the goods or services.
  • Merchant: the party the purchase is made from, who is legally responsible for providing the goods or services and receives the benefit of the payment.
  • Payment Handler: physically receives the payment from the Consumer on behalf of the Merchant.
  • Delivery Handler: physically delivers the goods or services on behalf of the Merchant.
  • Merchant Customer Care Provider: handles customer disputes and their resolution for the Merchant.

In the simplest case one merchant does everything. At the other extreme a merchant takes the order, tells the consumer to pay a bank, asks an overnight courier to deliver, and points the consumer to a 24x7 service if problems arise.
sections.eli5: Buying a toy can involve the shopkeeper, the cashier, the delivery driver and the helpdesk. They can all be one person or four different people, and the rules work either way.

sections.title: The Four Trading Exchanges
sections.content:
IOTP breaks a trade into four Trading Exchanges, each a swap of data between roles:

  • Offer: the Merchant tells the Consumer why the trade is happening. It is called an Offer because the Consumer must accept it for the trade to continue.
  • Payment: a payment between the Consumer and a Payment Handler, in either direction (a refund is a payment the other way).
  • Delivery: sends online goods, or delivery information about physical goods, from the Delivery Handler to the Consumer.
  • Authentication: lets any role check that another role is who it appears to be.

In the general payment case the Merchant sends a Brand List (payment brands, protocols and currency amounts on offer), the Consumer answers with a Brand Selection, the Merchant returns the payment details and optionally signs them, and the Consumer then sends a Payment Request to the Payment Handler. The payment scheme's own messages travel inside Pay Scheme Data components, and the Payment Handler finishes with a Payment Response carrying a receipt. To save round trips, components from several exchanges are packed into combined messages.

The Delivery Exchange ends with a Delivery Note, which can carry customer-care information such as a shipping tracking number, or the electronic goods themselves. The Authentication Exchange has an Authenticator that sends a challenge and an Authenticatee that answers it, followed by a Status component with the result.
sections.eli5: A trade is like four small chats: the shop shows you what you are buying, you pay, the goods come, and sometimes someone checks you are really you. IOTP writes down each chat.

sections.title: Messages, Blocks and Components
sections.content:
Every IOTP message is a well-formed XML document whose root element is IotpMessage. Inside it sit Trading Blocks, and each block holds a predefined set of Trading Components, the XML elements that carry the data for an exchange. Every message begins with a TransRefBlk (Transaction Reference Block) and may include an optional signature block and error block.

The Transaction Reference Block holds a TransId component that globally and uniquely identifies the transaction and is the same in every message of that transaction. It also holds a MsgId component that identifies the message, names the response it answers (RespIotpMsg), sets the language, and carries a SoftwareId that must include the manufacturer, software name, version and build. RelatedTo components can link a transaction to another transaction, such as a refund for an earlier purchase.

The IotpTransType attribute names which standard transaction is under way, and the Baseline values are BaselineAuthentication, BaselineDeposit, BaselinePurchase, BaselineRefund, BaselineWithdrawal, BaselineValueExchange, BaselineInquiry and BaselinePing.

Messages can travel over different transports. The RFC leaves transport details to separate supplements.
sections.eli5: An IOTP message is like a labeled folder. The cover says which trade it belongs to, and the pages inside hold the offer, the payment or the delivery details.

sections.title: IDs and Element References
sections.content:
Every message, block and component gets an XML ID attribute that is unique within one transaction and never changes, even when the element is copied into a later message. A component can therefore point at any other element in the transaction by using that value as an Element Reference, for example to name which Payment Handler organisation a payment uses.

The message ID is a prefix plus digits. The prefix is M for the Merchant or C for the Consumer, with I and Q used for inquiry or ping requests and responses respectively. Block and component IDs are the message ID, a dot and a number. As a guideline, the Consumer's second message is C2 and its first new component in that message is C2.1.
sections.eli5: Every page in the folder has a number stamped on it that never changes. If one page needs to talk about another, it just quotes the number.

sections.title: Extending IOTP and Packaged Content
sections.content:
IOTP elements form an XML namespace, so extra elements can be added at any level: new blocks, new components or new elements inside a component. New blocks and components must carry an ID. A reserved attribute, IOTP:Critical, tells a receiver what to do with an extension it does not understand. If it is True, the transaction has a Technical Error and must fail. If it is False, the transaction may continue, but the extra element must still be kept when copied and included in any signature digest. An extension with no such attribute is treated as True.

The Packaged Content element carries embedded data safely inside XML, such as payment scheme messages (SET messages, for example), or the description of an order, a payment note or a delivery note. Its Content attribute says what it holds (such as PCDATA, MIME or XML) and its Transform attribute is NONE or BASE64. Language is marked with xml:lang, and a message sender can list preferred languages and character sets, though the receiver need not honour them.
sections.eli5: If you want to add a new kind of note to the folder, you must mark it as either must-understand or safe-to-ignore. Odd objects go in a sealed envelope so they do not get squashed on the way.

sections.title: Error Handling and Idempotency
sections.content:
The RFC separates two kinds of failure. Technical errors are independent of the purpose of the message, such as malformed XML, and are reported in an Error Component inside an Error Block. Business errors, such as insufficient funds, belong to a process and are reported in the Status Component of the matching response block. No Error Component is generated for business errors.

An Error Component carries a Severity of Warning (the transaction can continue), TransientError (resending the message may fix it, with MinRetrySecs giving the minimum wait) or HardError (the transaction must stop). Errors can occur at the transport, message or block level. If a message holds several errors, the highest severity wins.

Because networks can deliver a message twice or not at all, IOTP requires idempotency: receiving the same state-changing request more than once must not repeat the action, so a customer pays an order only once. A server that receives an identical message again resends its earlier response, or answers with a MsgBeingProc transient error if the first is still being processed. The recommended way to compare messages is a DOM hash. A busy server can reply with a transient SystemBusy error. Because identical requests get identical replies, an up-to-date inquiry or ping needs a new message ID.

Any role can cancel a transaction by sending a message containing just a Cancel Block, but a Consumer should not cancel one that has already completed.
sections.eli5: If you press the pay button twice because the page is slow, you should only be charged once. IOTP also has three kinds of oops: a tiny one you can ignore, one where you try again, and one where you must stop.

sections.title: Signatures, Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Digital signatures in IOTP are entirely optional, and IOTP can work without them, although the RFC notes it is less secure in an open network. It is up to the Merchant to decide whether to sign, and up to the Consumer to decide whether an unsigned transaction is an acceptable risk. Reasons to sign include proving a merchant can be trusted, producing a record fit for a purpose such as tax authorities, and letting a Payment Handler know the amount was not altered. For example, without a signature a Consumer could change the amount due by removing a digit. Reasons not to sign include merged roles that can compare the data directly, and cryptography that costs too much for a payment of a few cents.

A Signature Component holds a Manifest of digests of other components, possibly including other signatures, in any message of the same transaction. Signing an Offer creates an Offer Response signature, which a Payment Handler later signs together with the payment record as a Payment Receipt signature. This binds the payment to the offer. Either symmetric or asymmetric cryptography may be used, even in one transaction, and the Consumer does not need to be given certificates.

Privacy is provided by sending messages over a secure channel such as SSL/TLS, which is optional. IOTP is blind to the payment protocol inside it, so it neither helps nor hinders payment security. That belongs in the payment protocol's own supplement.
sections.eli5: A signature is a seal on the note that shows nobody changed the price on the way. Sealing is optional, like deciding whether a small sticker is worth the effort.

sections.title: The Baseline Transactions
sections.content:
Baseline IOTP defines eight transaction types built from six Document Exchanges: Authentication, Brand Dependent Offer, Brand Independent Offer, Payment, Delivery, and Payment with Delivery. A Brand Dependent Offer lets the Merchant adapt the offer to the brand the Consumer picked, for instance to give a discount for using a store card.

  • Purchase: an optional authentication, an offer, then a payment and optionally a delivery.
  • Refund: an optional authentication, an offer and a payment from the Merchant to the Consumer.
  • Value Exchange: two payments that move value from one combination of currency and payment method to another.
  • Withdrawal and Deposit: taking electronic cash out of, or putting it into, a financial institution.
  • Authentication: one party checks another and may request its organisation details.
  • Inquiry: asks for the status of a transaction in progress or complete.
  • Ping: checks whether another IOTP application is running and whether signatures can be processed.

To claim to support IOTP, a solution must support all the transactions and blocks required of at least one role in the RFC's conformance table, which covers roles such as store merchants, e-cash issuers, consumers, payment handlers and delivery handlers. Elsewhere the RFC describes how logos are fetched in set sizes as GIF files, how brands (including dual and promotional brands) are chosen, and how codes are coordinated with IANA.
sections.eli5: There are eight kinds of play in this game, like buying, getting your money back, swapping coins, and asking if your parcel is on its way. Each one has its own order of steps.

children.note: same in every message of the transaction

messages.label: Brand List
messages.note: Payment brands, protocols and currency amounts on offer.

messages.label: Brand Selection
messages.note: The brand, protocol and amount the Consumer chose.

messages.label: Payment, Organisations
messages.note: Optionally signed to authorise the payment.

messages.label: PAYMENT EXCHANGE
messages.note: Pay Scheme Data from the payment protocol, exchanged in both directions.

items.label: Transaction continues
items.desc: There is a message in error, but the IOTP Transaction can still continue.

items.label: Retry later
items.desc: Resending the message in error may fix it; MinRetrySecs gives the minimum wait.

items.label: Transaction stops
items.desc: Unrecoverable error in the message; the IOTP Transaction must stop.
